chapters.title: Chapter 2: Building Blocks: Randomness, Volatility, and Brownian Motion

lessons.title: Modeling Stock Prices as Random Walks

children.text: Why Guessing Tomorrow's Price Is a Coin Flip

Nifty closed higher yesterday. Does that make it more likely to close higher again today, or does it make a pullback more likely? Pull up ten years of daily closes on screener.in or your broker's charting tool and test either theory, and you will find almost nothing useful: whether yesterday was up or down carries barely any information about today. Modern finance takes this observation and builds it into the very first assumption behind every option pricing model in this course: treat the next price move as if it were the flip of a coin.

body.text: This is not a throwaway simplification. It connects directly to the no-arbitrage argument from Chapter 1. If tomorrow's move were reliably predictable from today's price alone, traders would trade on that pattern until it stopped working, in the same way a mispriced option gets arbitraged away. Randomness, in this framework, is not the model giving up on forecasting. It is the model taking the market's own competitiveness seriously.

children.text: Building a Random Walk, One Coin Flip at a Time

is the simplest possible model of this idea. Start Nifty at 24,800. On each trading day, flip a fair coin: heads, Nifty moves up 50 points; tails, it moves down 50 points. Nothing about today's flip depends on yesterday's. Run ten flips and you get a concrete path.

markDefs.definition: A sequence of steps where each step's size and direction is random and independent of every step before it, so the path has no memory of where it has been.

body.title: The 10-day random walk from the table above

children.text: Five heads, five tails, and Nifty lands exactly back at 24,800. That was not fated to happen. Flip a different sequence and you land somewhere else entirely. The point of this exercise is not the ending level. It is that nothing in the process ever looks ahead or remembers a trend, yet it still produces a path that looks a lot like a real price chart, with rallies, pullbacks, and stretches that look deceptively like momentum.

body.title: The coin doesn't remember
body.textWithBlank: Because heads and tails are equally likely, the ___ of a single step in this random walk is zero: on average, the step neither adds nor removes value before it happens.
body.explanation: With a 50% chance of +50 and a 50% chance of −50, the expected value of one step is 0.5 × 50 + 0.5 × (−50) = 0. That does not mean the step will be zero. It means there is no built-in bias either way, which is exactly what "no free forecast" requires.

children.text: Independence: Why the Path So Far Doesn't Predict the Next Step

A random walk's defining property is independent increments: the size and direction of tomorrow's move does not depend on today's level, or on how you got there. Being at 24,850 after four flips carries no information about flip five. This directly contradicts a very common trading instinct.

body.title: The best forecast you have
body.question: If a stock price genuinely followed a pure random walk with zero drift, what is the single best forecast for tomorrow's price, using only today's price and its history?
options: A trend line extrapolated from the last five sessions
Today's closing price itself, since the expected next step is zero
The average of the last ten closing prices
Whatever direction the price has moved for three sessions in a row
body.explanation: With independent, zero-mean steps, no amount of staring at the past changes the expected future step. Today's price is your best forecast for tomorrow's, a property economists call a martingale. Trend lines and streak-chasing only feel informative; a pure random walk has already priced in everything they claim to reveal.

body.title: "It can't keep falling forever"
body.scenario: Nifty has closed lower for four straight sessions. On X, a trader posts that a bounce is "due" tomorrow because the index cannot keep falling forever, and urges followers to buy calls.
body.prompt: Using the independence property of a random walk, evaluate this trader's reasoning. Is there anything worth taking seriously in it, and anything that is simply wrong?
body.modelAnswer:
The literal claim, that four straight down days makes an up day more likely tomorrow, is the gambler's fallacy. A coin does not owe you heads after four tails, and under a pure random walk with independent increments, four down days carry zero predictive information about day five. The model has no memory, so "it's due" is not a real edge.

What is worth taking seriously is that real markets are not guaranteed to be a perfect random walk at every timescale. Some studies do find short-term momentum or mean-reversion effects in certain markets and periods. The honest response is not to blindly assume randomness either, but to test the specific claim on data before trading on it, rather than accepting a gut feeling that a losing streak must end. Lesson 2.4 comes back to exactly this: which assumptions behind these models are convenient simplifications, and where real markets quietly disagree with them.

children.text: The Flaw This Simple Walk Still Has

This coin-flip walk is a useful first sketch, but it has a flaw that becomes obvious the moment you push it far enough. Every step is a fixed ₹50, or fixed 50 points, regardless of the price level. A stock at ₹20 and a stock at ₹2,000 would both take the same rupee-sized steps in this model, which makes no sense: a ₹50 move means something very different to each of them. Worse, run this walk long enough with a long enough string of unlucky tails, and the model lets the price wander below zero, something no real share price, and no real index, can ever do.

body.label: The additive walk's blind spot
body.value: Fixed rupee steps, any price level
body.context: A model where step size never scales with price treats a ₹50 move on a ₹20 stock the same as on Nifty at 24,800, and cannot rule out a negative price. Lesson 2.2 fixes both problems at once by switching from fixed rupee steps to percentage steps.

body.text: A random walk is not the model admitting defeat on forecasting. It is the model taking seriously that a competitive market has already erased any pattern simple enough for you to trade on.

points: A random walk models each price step as random and independent of every step before it, with no memory of the path so far.
This connects to Chapter 1's no-arbitrage logic: if a pattern in past prices reliably predicted future ones, competitive trading would erase it.
A zero-drift random walk has an expected step of zero, making today's price the best forecast for tomorrow's, a property called a martingale.
The gambler's fallacy, expecting a bounce simply because a losing streak has gone on, has no basis in a true random walk's independent increments.
This simple walk still has a flaw: fixed rupee-sized steps ignore the price level and can push prices below zero, which Lesson 2.2's geometric version fixes.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. The Nifty levels, coin-flip sequence, and the trader scenario are hypothetical illustrations of random walk mechanics, not live market data or trading signals.
